title: Headroom Marketplace & Provisioning — PRD sketch
body:
Context / problem

We currently offer dedicated pools + burst credits and a set of heuristics for tenant isolation. Customers repeatedly ask for predictable, on-demand headroom without the friction of long-term commits or brittle burst policies: e.g., sudden campaign traffic, holiday spikes, model evaluation runs. Existing burst credit systems either (a) require front-loaded reservations, (b) provide blunt throttles that cause customer-visible errors, or (c) leak capacity fairness and complicate ops.

Goal (what success looks like)

- Provide a self-serve, low-friction mechanism for tenants to request short-lived capacity above their reserved baseline with clear economic and isolation semantics.
- Keep tail latency and core SLOs for committed tenants intact (isolate noisy surges).
- Make operational control and observability simple: per-tenant accounting, rollback, and automated reclaiming after spike.
- Enable product experimentation: price signals, soft auctions, and priority lanes for critical jobs.

Non-goals

- Not trying to replace long-term reserved capacity contracts.
- Not a full multi-tenant marketplace for arbitrary spot trading between customers (phase 1 will centralize management and limits).

Proposal overview: "Headroom Marketplace" (phase 1: managed headroom pool)

We propose a managed headroom pool paired with a tenant-facing provisioning API and UI that allows tenants to:
  - allocate “headroom reservations” (HRs) of short duration (minutes → hours) on top of their committed baseline, billed by consumption or time-window;
  - optionally attach priority / QoS labels (latency-critical, best-effort, background) to each HR;
  - set automated replenish policies: e.g., maintain X minutes of headroom at all times, or only top-up when predicted demand > threshold;
  - observe billing & telemetry for each HR; headroom usage is measured at token-per-compute and request-lane granularity.

Key behavioral primitives

1) Soft reservations: HRs act like ephemeral reservations. They grant the tenant access to a slice of managed pool capacity for a time window. If pool is saturated, HRs degrade according to priority (best-effort trimmed first).

2) Priority lanes: HRs can request a lane tag (hot/standard/cold). Hot lanes have faster prewarm and lower throttling, cost premium.

3) Grace credits & failover: every HR optionally includes a small grace credit bucket to absorb short bursts under network noise. If headroom is exhausted, traffic falls back to baseline model variants or queued with a configurable TTL.

4) Central budget & per-tenant caps: to prevent noisy-neighbor abuses, an account-level budget/cap limits total concurrent HRs. Ops can set global guardrails per region.

Architecture components (high level)

- Provisioning API & UI (Console): create/list HRs, attach policies, preview cost.
- Headroom allocator (control plane): decides whether to grant HRs at request time based on pool utilization, per-tenant caps, historical usage, and priority.
- Runtime admission & shaping (runtime sidecar/adaptor): enforces lane semantics, prewarm signals, and traffic shaping for fallback.
- Billing & metering: charge by time-window + consumption; record per-HR telemetry (tokens, latency percentiles, errors).
- Policy engine for soft auctions: a simple scoring model for competing HR grants when pool tight.

APIs (sketch)

POST /v1/dedicated/headroom-reservations
Request body (example):
{
  "tenant_id": "acme",
  "duration_minutes": 60,
  "max_qps": 200,
  "lane": "hot",
  "billing_model": "consumption", // consumption | time-window
  "replenish_policy": "never" // never | auto | predictive
}

Response (granted / queued / denied) with reason and estimated cost.

Operational behavior examples

- Normal case: tenant requests 60m HR for hot lane; allocator grants immediately and runtime prewarms an extra 2 nodes; traffic uses HR and is metered.
- Pool constrained: two simultaneous HR requests; priority scoring grants one; second request queued with ETA and optional auto-accept when capacity frees.
- Graceful degradation: HR ends or exhausted → runtime shifts tenant traffic to baseline model variant (lower throughput but preserved correctness) and enqueues telemetry event for ops.

SLOs & metrics

- Availability: HR grant decision latency < 500ms (for interactive requests).
- Latency impact: 99th percentile tail for committed-tenants must not regress > 10% while any HRs are active.
- Economic: average cost per headroom-minute within X% of forecasted pricing (measured after 2 months).
- Adoption: pilot with 5 customers & >=20 HRs/day across them in month 1.

Rollout plan (phases)

Phase 0: internal playground
- Manual allocator toggles, single-region, no billing (ops only).
- Heavy instrumentation.

Phase 1: closed-beta customers
- Expose console + API, simple time-window billing, per-tenant caps, and basic priority lanes.
- Metrics dashboard and runbook.

Phase 2: pricing experiments & limited marketplace features
- Introduce consumption billing and soft-auction price multiplier, run A/B pricing experiments.

Phase 3: wider availability
- Region parity, self-serve pricing, fine-grained policy templates.

Operational playbook (ops runbook sketch)

- If pool utilization > 85% sustained (10m avg): enable temporary higher eviction thresholds, notify customers with active HRs, and open warm nodes.
- If grant latency > 500ms: scale control-plane horizontally, degrade scoring to simpler heuristics until healthy.
- If tail latency of committed tenants regresses > 10%: trigger emergency clamp: pause new HRs for 15 minutes while preserving existing commitments; notify SRE/product.

Security & compliance notes

- HRs do not change data residency guarantees; headroom nodes created for HRs must honor tenant VPC/network constraints in private deployments.
- Billing traces and telemetry must be encrypted and retained according to enterprise retention settings.

Open questions / risks (to discuss)

- Pricing model: time-window vs consumption vs hybrid? Customers may prefer predictability (time-window) for campaigns; consumption better for sporadic tests.
- Predictive replenishment accuracy: how often do we mis-forecast and cause surprise charges or failed grants?
- Behavioral risk: will tenants try to game the system by spiky load to push others out? Need stronger per-account caps and fraud detection.

Next steps / short-term TODOs

- Sync with SRE (Marco) and runtime (Anneke) on prewarm mechanics and admission hooks — scheduled 2025-09-12.
- Prototype provisioning UI flow + API stub (owner: Priya) — 2 week spike.
- Define initial pricing bands and pilot customer contract language (Carlos to draft).
- Create JIRA epic with sub-tasks for control-plane, runtime, billing, and console.

Notes to self / rough ideas

- Could eventually expose an "offload" lane where non-critical inference can be executed on cheaper quantized variants in exchange for lower priority (interesting for cost-conscious customers).
- Consider an internal marketplace where customers can optionally sell unused HRs back to the pool at a discount (phase 3).

References

- See related plays: CONFLUENCE:DedicatedBurstGuidelines (historic ideas), JIRA-DEDIC-4018 (elastic pockets research).

—— end of sketch ———
